opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that post-training is fundamentally a thin layer on top of whatever the model learned during pre-training. When we try to bolt agentic capabilities on at the end, through supervised fine-tuning on agent trajectories or reinforcement learning on a handful of environments, we're asking a relatively small amount of data and compute to teach behaviors that are actually quite deep. Things like planning over long horizons, recovering from mistakes, knowing when to call a tool versus reason internally, keeping track of state across many steps. Those aren't surface-level formatting behaviors the way instruction following largely is.

What we see in practice is that post-training is very good at eliciting capabilities that are already latent in the base model. If the pre-trained model has seen enough examples of something resembling multi-step reasoning or interaction, post-training can sharpen it and make it reliable. But if the underlying representations just aren't there, post-training tends to produce brittle behavior. The model learns to imitate the shape of an agent trajectory without really internalizing the skills, so it works on distributions close to what it was tuned on and then falls apart when the environment changes a little, or the task gets longer, or something unexpected happens partway through.

There's also a data problem. Pre-training data is overwhelmingly static text: documents, web pages, code files. It's very rarely the record of an agent acting in the world, observing consequences, and adjusting. So the model's priors are shaped around predicting the next token of a finished artifact, not around taking actions and dealing with feedback. If you only introduce interactive, action-oriented data at the very end, you're fighting against everything the model learned before.

So my view is that if we really want capable agents, we need to think about agentic behavior much earlier in the pipeline: what goes into pre-training and mid-training, how we represent tool use and environment interaction in the data, how we build long-context and long-horizon reasoning into the base model itself. Post-training is still important, it's where you align and refine, but it shouldn't be where the fundamental capability is supposed to come from. Treating it that way puts a ceiling on how far these systems can go.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that post-training is fundamentally about shaping and steering capabilities that are already present in the base model. When you do supervised fine-tuning or RL on top of a pretrained model, you're really teaching it how to express what it already knows in a particular format, or how to prefer certain behaviors over others. You're not fundamentally creating new knowledge or new reasoning abilities from scratch.

And when we think about what agentic AI actually requires, it's a pretty different set of skills than what most pretraining data captures. You need the model to plan over long horizons, to decompose a task into steps, to take an action, observe what happened in the environment, and then update its plan based on that feedback. It has to recover from errors. It has to know when to call a tool versus when to reason on its own. And most of the data on the internet is static text. It's the output of human thought, not the process. So you don't see the trajectory of someone trying something, failing, and adjusting. That process data is just very sparse in the pretraining corpus.

So if you rely only on post-training to bolt agentic behaviors onto a model, you're working within the ceiling that pretraining gave you. You can get pretty far, and people have, but you start to see brittleness. The model does well on the distribution of tasks you trained on, and then it degrades when the environment looks a little different, or the horizon gets a little longer, or there's a tool it hasn't seen. You end up patching one behavior at a time, and that doesn't scale.

The other piece is that post-training data is expensive. If you're collecting human demonstrations of multi-step agentic trajectories or building reward models for them, that's orders of magnitude more costly per example than scraping text. So you're always going to be data-limited in that stage.

That's why I think the more interesting direction is to push some of these capabilities earlier in the pipeline, whether that's through synthetic trajectory data in pretraining, or mid-training stages, or environments where the model can actually interact and learn from the consequences of its actions at scale. You want the agentic priors to be baked into the representations, so that post-training is doing alignment and refinement rather than carrying the entire burden of teaching the model how to act in the world.

astra-6.text:
I think post-training is a very powerful tool, but it’s limited by what the underlying model has learned. If we start with a model trained primarily to predict the next token, and then expect post-training to give it planning, tool use, and the ability to recover from mistakes over a long sequence of actions, we’re asking that stage to do a lot.

For an agent, the challenge isn’t just producing a good response. It’s taking an action, observing what changed, and deciding what to do next. And sometimes you don’t know whether an action was useful until many steps later. That makes both learning and assigning credit much harder.

So I see this as a question about the whole training pipeline. How do we give models experience with interaction and sequential decision-making earlier? Post-training still has an important role, but I wouldn’t assume that we can leave the rest of the training recipe unchanged and get all of those capabilities at the end.

sol-6.1.text:
I think post-training is very powerful, but it’s operating on top of the capabilities and representations that the model has already learned. If we want a model to plan, take actions, observe what happened, and revise its approach over a long horizon, we’re asking for something quite different from predicting the next token in a document.

If we leave all of that to post-training, we’re asking a relatively small part of the training process to bridge that gap. And the feedback becomes challenging: an agent might take many steps before you know whether it succeeded. How do you assign credit to the decisions along the way?

So I wouldn’t say post-training is the wrong approach. I’d say we should also ask what needs to change earlier—in the data, the training objectives, and the environments the model learns from—so that interaction and learning from consequences are part of the foundation. Then post-training can build on those capabilities.
